extracted.intended_audience: NIH grant applicants (UW School of Nursing investigators and similar researchers preparing research project grant applications)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing NIH research project grant applications aligned to the NIH Simplified Review Framework (SRF): emphasize importance, demonstrate rigor and feasibility, and show appropriate expertise/resources. Includes scoring expectations and applicant-facing advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of the Research
rubrics_metrics.description: Should this research be done? If so, why? (Framing described as 'Importance of the Research' under the SRF.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must clearly articulate the scientific importance of their work—not just its relevance to public health. This means: framing the research question in a compelling way; demonstrating how the work addresses a significant gap in knowledge; avoiding jargon and making the case accessible to a broad scientific audience. A clear, persuasive rationale for the study’s importance can set the tone for the entire review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigor and Feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Can it be done well? If so, How? (SRF factor focused on methodological soundness and feasibility.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers are encouraged to avoid nitpicking and instead focus on whether the proposed approach is rigorous and feasible. Applicants should present a well-structured, logical plan; anticipate potential challenges and describe how they’ll be addressed; and emphasize methodological soundness without overwhelming the reader with excessive detail. The goal is to instill confidence that the research can be executed effectively even if every contingency isn’t fully mapped out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expertise and Resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the right people and tools in place to do it? (SRF factor assessing team qualifications and access to resources.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This factor is no longer numerically scored but is evaluated as either 'appropriate' or 'additional expertise/resources needed,' with comments required only if gaps are identified. Applicants should clearly describe the qualifications of the team as they relate to the project; highlight access to necessary facilities, equipment, and institutional support; avoid over-relying on reputation; and focus on relevance and readiness. This change is designed to reduce reputational bias and level the playing field for newer investigators and institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring and evaluation format under SRF
rubrics_metrics.description: How reviewers will score the three core factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each of the first two factors (Importance; Rigor and Feasibility) is scored on a 1–9 scale. The third factor (Expertise and Resources) is evaluated categorically as 'appropriate' or 'additional expertise/resources needed.' Comments for the third factor are required only when gaps are identified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduced emphasis on ancillary/administrative criteria ('Less Is More')
rubrics_metrics.description: SRF reduces burden of additional review criteria so reviewers can stay focused on core scientific questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While issues like human subjects protections can still affect the overall impact score, other items — such as budget and resource authentication — no longer affect the impact score. Applicants should therefore focus on core scientific priorities and avoid overloading proposals with administrative minutiae that reviewers are being asked to deprioritize.

rubrics_metrics.name: SRF objectives: fairness, clarity, scientific focus, and reduced bias/fatigue
rubrics_metrics.description: Rationale driving the SRF: address overemphasis on technical minutiae, inadequate attention to significance and innovation, bias toward well-known investigators/institutions, and review fatigue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should align proposals with SRF goals by emphasizing scientific importance and feasibility, and by demonstrating team readiness in ways that do not rely on reputation alone. Understanding these objectives helps applicants prioritize what reviewers are being asked to value.
